component.name: Cycle
component.summary: Indoor cycling training with smart trainer control

description.p: Cycle is a GNOME application for indoor cycling training. It connects to BLE smart trainers via FTMS, lets you run structured ERG workouts, records sessions with power, heart rate, and cadence data, and provides AI coaching advice through the Claude API.
Features:

ul.li: BLE smart trainer control via FTMS (ERG mode)
Structured workout player with power zone visualisation
Session recording: power, heart rate, cadence
AI coaching suggestions powered by the Anthropic Claude API

screenshot.caption: Riding a structured workout in ERG mode
Fitness, fatigue and form over time
The training week at a glance
Coaching notes written for the ride ahead
What a planned session asks of you
Pairing a smart trainer and sensors

description.p: Your outdoor rides now count towards your plan. A day you actually trained on is no longer read as a missed session, whatever your plan had asked for that day — Cycle already holds the ride and no longer needs to be told about it. Nothing to tap, and nothing claims a road ride was an interval workout: opening the day shows you what it found. On this rider's own history it turned twelve missed sessions into eight, and only the genuinely skipped days are still counted.

When your program eases a session more than once, Undo now steps back one change at a time instead of jumping straight to the original. Before, the workout in between was lost and could not be reached from either direction. The row tells you where a press will land, while still naming what your program first asked for.
Opening a planned workout on the calendar now shows its power profile, so you can see the shape of a session where you decide whether to ride it — including on days you have already finished.
The load shown for a day you marked done no longer counts the same training twice when a real ride is sitting on it.

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v5 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.6.1 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.

Your ANT+ trainer is found again when you switch it on after opening Cycle. The ANT stick was only ever given 25 seconds to look for it, and once that ran out it quietly stopped listening for the rest of the session. A trainer woken a minute later was never seen, and pressing Scan did not bring it back — the only cure was restarting the app with the trainer already awake.

Cycle now keeps looking for as long as it is open, and if a search does stop, it notices and starts it again. Your heart rate strap and cadence sensor were affected in the same way and are fixed with it, so switching any of them on late now works.

You can now mark a planned session done yourself. Most riding happens away from this app, and until now a session only closed if you rode that exact workout here, on the day it was planned. Open a day on the calendar, or use the week list or your program card, and say the session happened. Ticked the wrong day, or changed your mind? Mark it not done again.

Marking a session done settles your plan and nothing else. It banks no training load: your fitness is worked out from rides that were actually recorded, never from the calendar. The day's load bar will fill in, because that is your plan's own accounting — but your fitness and form do not move.

Missed sessions are now counted over the last fortnight rather than over the whole program. If you started a plan with a date already in the past, it was counting sessions you never had the chance to ride, and that number could never come down however well you trained. Your coach is told the same fortnight, so it plans around the rider you are now rather than one who appears to have stopped.
On the week view, Undo now has a row of its own instead of sitting beside Apply, where it was not clear which change it would undo.
Your calendar now shows which sessions belong to your training program. Look for the accent dot in the month view; the week view spells out which week of the plan each session falls in.

When your program wants to ease a session — because your form is dug in, your resting heart rate is up, or you have missed a run of sessions — the calendar says so on the day itself, explains why, and lets you apply the change without leaving the page. Changed your mind? Undo puts the session back to what the plan originally asked for.
As before, adjustments only ever make a session easier, and only ever the next one: your form is worked out afresh every day, so deciding Thursday's session today would be guessing.
You can now plan a GPX route on the calendar, not just a workout. A planned route counts towards your projected fitness, using an estimate of what riding it will cost.
Anything you have planned can be moved. Drag it to another day in the week or month view, or open it and choose Reschedule. Sessions you have already ridden stay where they are.

Choosing what to schedule now shows you what you are picking: a workout's shape, length and training load, a route's distance and climbing, and what your training plan expects that day. There is a search box for finding something in a large library.
Cycle also asks for less access to your computer than before. It no longer requests any filesystem access at all.

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v4 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.3.0 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.
Cycle now shows screenshots in GNOME Software.
Updated a networking library to pick up an upstream thread-safety fix.
Fixed the first-run setup wizard, which opened too small and did not apply what you entered.
Initial release.
